source: OWASP Top 10:2025 (A03 Software Supply Chain Failures & A08 Software/Data Integrity Failures)

rules.name: A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures
rules.description: New category for 2025, expanding the prior 'vulnerable and outdated components' concept to cover breakdowns or compromises anywhere in the process of building, distributing, or updating software, including third-party dependencies, build systems, CI/CD pipelines, and update mechanisms.

rules.name: Use of Obsolete Function
rules.description: A dependency or codebase relies on a function or API that has been deprecated or superseded, often because the replacement addresses a known security weakness the obsolete version lacks.

rules.name: Use of Unmaintained Third-Party Components
rules.description: The software depends on a third-party component that is no longer actively maintained, meaning newly discovered vulnerabilities or malicious takeovers of that component may never be patched.

rules.name: Reliance on Component That is Not Updateable
rules.description: The software depends on a component that cannot easily be patched or replaced once deployed, extending the window during which a compromise in that component remains exploitable.

rules.name: Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component
rules.description: The software incorporates a third-party component with a known vulnerability, inheriting that weakness into every downstream consumer of the software.

rules.name: Self-Propagating Credential-Stealing Package Worm
rules.description: A real-world pattern (e.g. the 2025-2026 'Shai-Hulud' npm campaigns) in which a compromised package's install script harvests credentials (npm, GitHub, cloud provider tokens) from the host, exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled location, and then uses the stolen publishing credentials to automatically backdoor further packages the victim maintains - achieving self-replicating, worm-like spread across a package ecosystem.

rules.name: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures
rules.description: Focuses on failures to verify the integrity or provenance of software and data artifacts at the point of use - a narrower, more granular concern than the end-to-end Software Supply Chain Failures category - covering cases like unsigned updates, unvetted plugins, or CI/CD pipelines accepting artifacts without verification.

rules.name: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
rules.description: The software imports or includes executable functionality (such as a library or remote script) from a source outside its intended trust boundary, without verifying its integrity or origin.

rules.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
rules.description: The application allows external input to control which object properties get set or modified at runtime (e.g. mass-assignment or prototype-pollution-style flaws), potentially allowing an attacker to override security-relevant internal state.

rules.name: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
rules.description: The application deserializes data from an untrusted source without sufficiently validating it first, which can allow an attacker to construct a malicious serialized object that executes arbitrary code upon deserialization.

rules.name: Installation of a Package from an Untrusted, Unsigned Source
rules.description: A developer, unable to find an expected package version through the official, trusted package manager, downloads it instead from an unofficial website. The package is unsigned, so its integrity cannot be verified, and it contains malicious code - an OWASP-documented scenario that is the direct subject of supply-chain malware detection.
